description: We are a group of students from Medellín interested in space, engineering, and science. This is our first time participating in a hackathon, and we are very excited about the hackathon's connection with NASA.
summary: We developed a website that both NASA and various industries can use to find specific information about Earth's topography, climate parameters, and other environmental variables, allowing them to locate sites worldwide for their projects. For NASA, it could be useful for finding locations in the Americas to create and test new instruments and vehicles for future NASA missions. For agriculture, it can help locate suitable sites for planting specific seeds.
details: S.E.I.A.T is a web tool that finds the places on Earth that best mimic the conditions of the Moon or Mars, so that rovers, space structures, and other exploration hardware can be tested on Earth before flight. We obtained maps and files from NASA’s Giovanni (Earthdata) portal for five variables across the Americas: temperature, humidity, albedo, day–night temperature swing, and wind speed. These feed a multi-objective optimization model that combines Pareto-front filtering with a weighted Chebyshev score, minimizing the largest weighted gap between each location and the desired conditions. On the website, users set a target value and an importance weight for each variable, choose one of three preset Moon and Mars missions, or describe their mission in plain words and let an AI model translate it into specific targets and weights. The model then returns the best-matching coordinates. This makes site selection transparent, customizable, and data-driven instead of based on tradition, and it gives Latin American teams access to nearby analog sites. The approach also scales beyond space: agriculture could find zones suited to a specific crop, and construction could check whether a location is suitable for a given building. The website was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and the mathematical model and data processing were written in Python. We limited the model to five variables and to the Americas to save computing resources and time, and because that region offered enough NASA data to work with reliably.
